title: Review: Polysaccharides; Elements, monomers and condensation/hydrolysis; Lipids: triglycerides; Phospholipids, steroids and other lipids; Protein structure and function; Amino acids and peptide bonds
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM04#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM02#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM06#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM08a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM02#N.8a, BM04#N.6, BM05#N.3, BM06#N.4, BM07#N.6a, BM08a#N.4a, BM02#N.10a, BM04#N.8, BM05#N.14, BM06#N.14, BM07#N.13, BM08a#N.13. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Glycogen
items.clue: The energy store found in animals and fungi

items.label: Polymer
items.clue: A large molecule made of many small units joined together

items.label: Hydrophilic
items.clue: Describes the charged phosphate head, which interacts with water

items.label: Primary structure
items.clue: The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, held by peptide bonds

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?

options.text: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used

questions.explanation: An –OH from one monomer and an –H from the other combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers.

questions.stem: Liver cells store glucose in the form of glycogen. Why is the glucose not simply stored as free glucose?

options.text: Glycogen is insoluble because it is non-polar, so it stays separate from the watery cytoplasm
The branches of glycogen make its glucose hard to remove, so the store is not used up too quickly
Glycogen is relatively insoluble because of its size, so it does not affect the osmotic balance of the cell
Glycogen stores extra energy in the glycosidic bonds that link its glucose monomers together

questions.explanation: Glycogen is very large and relatively insoluble, so much can be stored without raising the solute concentration of the cytoplasm. Free glucose would draw water in by osmosis.

questions.stem: One glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules react by condensation to form one triglyceride. How much water is produced?

options.text: One water molecule is released
Three water molecules are released
Four water molecules are released
No water is released; water is used up

questions.explanation: Each –OH of glycerol reacts with the carboxyl group of one fatty acid in a separate condensation, forming an ester bond and releasing one water: three in total.

questions.stem: Which components are linked together by condensation reactions to form one phospholipid molecule?

options.text: One glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphate group
One glycerol, three fatty acids and one phosphate group
Three glycerol molecules, one fatty acid and one phosphate group
Many fatty acid monomers joined in a chain, plus one phosphate group

questions.explanation: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups. In a phospholipid two of them are linked by condensation to fatty acids and the third to a phosphate group, giving two hydrophobic tails and a hydrophilic head.

questions.stem: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?

options.text: 150 released
298 released
149 released
149 consumed

questions.explanation: Each condensation forms one peptide bond and releases one water molecule. A chain of 150 needs 149 bonds: 149 water molecules.

questions.stem: What stabilises the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
Ionic bonds between charged amine and carboxyl groups spaced regularly along the backbone.
Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.
Hydrogen bonds forming the peptide links between the amine and carboxyl groups of neighbours.

questions.explanation: Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one peptide bond and the N–H of another, at regular positions along the backbone.

questions.stem: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?

options.text: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules

questions.explanation: 100 amino acids are joined by 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, split to supply the –H and –OH.

questions.stem: Cellulose gives plant cell walls high tensile strength. Which feature of cellulose is responsible for this?

options.text: Straight chains lie side by side in bundles, cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds
The glycosidic bonds within cellulose are very much stronger than those within starch
The chains coil into tight helices that stretch and recoil like a spring
Beta-glucose is a larger monomer than alpha-glucose, giving thicker chains

questions.explanation: Straight, unbranched chains of β-glucose pack side by side in bundles linked by very many hydrogen bonds. Each is weak; together they resist stretching.

questions.stem: To make a spread, manufacturers react a liquid vegetable oil with hydrogen, using a catalyst. Some C=C double bonds in its fatty acid chains become C–C single bonds. How does the oil change?

options.text: It becomes more liquid, as double bonds stiffen chains and hold molecules together.
It becomes more unsaturated, as it now carries more hydrogen atoms.
It becomes more solid, as straighter chains pack more closely together.
It becomes more solid, as the extra bonds need more heat to break when it melts.

questions.explanation: Fewer kinks, closer packing, stronger attractions between molecules: a higher melting point. A liquid oil becomes a soft solid, like butter in the hook.

questions.stem: Lipoproteins carry cholesterol and triglycerides in blood plasma, which is mostly water. Each lipoprotein has an oily core of cholesterol and triglyceride, surrounded by a single layer of phospholipids (with some proteins). How are the phospholipids in this layer most likely arranged?

options.text: Tails facing outwards into the plasma; heads facing inwards into the oily core.
Heads facing outwards into the plasma; tails pointing inwards into the oily core.
Tails joined to one another by covalent bonds, forming a rigid shell around the core.
Mixed evenly through the oily core, as phospholipids are entirely hydrophobic like cholesterol.

questions.stem: Two short polypeptides, P and Q, are each made of the same five amino acids, but the amino acids are joined in a different order in P and in Q. Which statement about P and Q is correct?

options.text: They are the same molecule, because they contain exactly the same amino acids.
They have the same properties, because a polypeptide's properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.
They are different polypeptides, because their R groups sit in different positions along the chain.
They are different polypeptides, because their peptide bonds join different pairs of R groups.

questions.explanation: Each chain has four peptide bonds and the same backbone, but the R groups are in a different order. Order is one of the three sources of variety, with chain length and repeats.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme at a position on the surface far from the active site in the folded protein. The enzyme loses most of its activity. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The result must be an error, because only the amino acids of the active site itself can affect catalysis
The change disturbs interactions that hold the enzyme's overall shape, altering the active site
The loss of activity shows the enzyme has been denatured, so its chain has broken up into free amino acids
The changed amino acid supplies less energy to the reaction, so the substrate cannot react
